concept: Shared-cost allocation rules for managed database services
summary: Source-anchored research for Shared-cost allocation rules for managed database services. Run status: COMPLETED.

facts.text: Costfluent recommends storage per tenant plus query time for a shared relational database where load differs, noting that storage alone understates compute-heavy tenants, and warns that a request says nothing about its compute effort. Costfluent describes these as its own recommendations. Sources: https://costfluent.com/blog/multi-tenant-saas-cost-allocation

An auditable allocation should preserve the source total: recipient shares plus explicitly retained central, idle and unallocated amounts must reconcile to each component’s cost. Use one cost basis, align usage and cost periods, and document changes to allocation rules. These are proposed controls for the Atlas allocation pipeline. (medium confidence)

Atlas billing FAQ states that resource tags on invoice CSVs and Admin API responses reflect the tags configured when the CSV is generated or API is invoked, including only the latest configuration after changes within a billing cycle. For reproducible historical allocation, preserve extraction-time metadata and an effective-dated allocation-rule history outside the mutable tag view. The preservation step is an inference from the documented behavior. (low confidence) (verified as of 2026-10-18)

The University of Washington paper How to Price Shared Optimizations in the Cloud studies sharing the cost of database indexes and materialized views among users. It proposes mechanism-design approaches, including a Shapley Value Mechanism for an offline additive setting and extensions for changing users and substitutive optimizations. Its truthfulness and cost-recovery results concern those models; they do not establish a universal Atlas chargeback formula. (low confidence) Sources: https://arxiv.org/abs/1203.0059 ; https://cloud-data-pricing.cs.washington.edu

The FinOps Foundation tenant-traffic case allocates shared cost by each tenant's share of requests, taken from a tenant ID field in application logs and combined with daily AWS cost data by a custom script. A request-share split is a proxy: the FinOps Framework notes shared costs can be allocated using proxy metrics, and that observability or utilization data can enable more granular allocation of shared cost elements. Sources: https://www.finops.org/assets/how-to-allocate-shared-cost-based-on-traffic/ ; https://www.finops.org/framework/capabilities/allocation

Azure's prefilled proportional percentages remain fixed until someone manually updates the rule, even when initially derived from target compute, storage, network, or total costs. A rule described as proportional therefore does not necessarily recalculate its weights continuously; refresh cadence must be explicit. (low confidence) (verified as of 2025-06-27)

For shared, multi-tenant resources, resource tags identify the cost pool but not each tenant's share; the FinOps traffic-based case study (Tenerity India) takes the tenant ID field from application logs to compute each tenant's share of traffic and applies it to daily costs fetched by resource tags. FinOps also notes that allocation of shared cost elements can use observability or utilization data. Sources: https://www.finops.org/assets/how-to-allocate-shared-cost-based-on-traffic/ ; https://www.finops.org/framework/capabilities/allocation

Valid shared-cost policies include fixed allocations, even splits, proportional (usage-based) splits and central funding. The FinOps Framework advises choosing, for each shared cost, the allocation policy that gives the best value, and notes that most organizations mix allocation to cost-center budgets with central funding. Sources: https://www.finops.org/framework/capabilities/allocation

Shared managed-database allocation needs an explicit policy in addition to resource tags: identify the shared cost pool, its beneficiaries, its allocation basis and any amount funded centrally. Tags identify ownership or pools; usage or other contextual data determines how a shared pool is split. This is a design recommendation for Atlas showback, not a claim that Atlas computes tenant-level splits. (high confidence)

For a usage-proportional pool, allocate recipient cost as pool cost multiplied by recipient measured usage divided by total measured usage for that pool and period. AWS demonstrates this arithmetic using network bytes, while a Tenerity practitioner describes applying tenant request shares to tag-selected daily resource costs. These are examples to adapt, not evidence that request counts equal database resource consumption. (high confidence) Sources: https://aws.amazon.com/blogs/aws-cloud-financial-management/gs-chargeback-shared-services-an-aws-transit-gateway-example/ ; https://www.finops.org/assets/how-to-allocate-shared-cost-based-on-traffic/

Shared-cost rules can use fixed percentages, equal splits, or proportional usage. The organization should choose the method for each pool; AWS's chargeback guidance explicitly separates identifying cost units, calculating shared costs, selecting distribution logic, and collecting allocation data. (high confidence) Sources: https://www.finops.org/framework/capabilities/allocation ; https://aws.amazon.com/blogs/aws-cloud-financial-management/gs-chargeback-shared-services-an-aws-transit-gateway-example/

Full direct chargeback is optional. An organization can deliberately fund selected shared services centrally and report them through showback. Nationwide describes this approach for residual enterprise expenses, consistent with the FinOps framework's centrally budgeted shared-cost option. (high confidence) Sources: https://www.finops.org/assets/avoid-and-simplify-shared-costs/ ; https://www.finops.org/framework/capabilities/allocation

Reducing ambiguity upstream can simplify allocation: Nationwide assigns accounts a default cost center and sometimes dedicates clusters to a department or application. FinOps guidance likewise uses account structures and ownership metadata before introducing more granular shared-cost mechanisms. (high confidence)

AWS's four-step chargeback design is: decide the cost units to charge back to, calculate the total cost of the shared service, choose a distribution logic (equitable or proportional), and gather the data to charge back accurately. The FinOps Allocation capability includes defining and maintaining a strategy to document apportionment of shared costs and impacts to allocation targets. Retaining the original shared-cost total, recipient mapping, distribution logic and supporting measurements as audit records is this report's own recommended practice, not a requirement stated by either source. Sources: https://aws.amazon.com/blogs/aws-cloud-financial-management/gs-chargeback-shared-services-an-aws-transit-gateway-example/ ; https://www.finops.org/framework/capabilities/allocation

Microsoft's cost-allocation rules do not alter the Azure invoice or billing responsibility. They create internal allocation entries; invoice reconciliation filters those entries out. This illustrates why an Atlas chargeback ledger should preserve supplier billing separately from internal redistribution. (low confidence) (verified as of 2025-06-27)
